title: MAMA DIDN’T LEAVE ME JUNK — SHE LEFT ME A TRAP
excerpt: My sister Wanda said it with a laugh as she shoved another cardboard box into the back of her SUV.
author: admin

blocks.text: My sister Wanda said it with a laugh as she shoved another cardboard box into the back of her SUV.

She was standing in the middle of our mother’s living room, wearing a cream-colored designer sweater, expensive sunglasses, and the satisfied expression of someone who had just won a game nobody else knew they were playing.
Behind her, movers were carrying out the antique dining table, the leather sofa, and a beautiful oak cabinet that had stood beside Mama’s fireplace for nearly forty years.
Wanda had already claimed the house furnishings and the $130,000 in savings.
My older brother, Charles, got the forty acres of farmland outside town.

And me? I got twelve chipped ceramic jars shaped like roosters, pigs, chickens, and other farm animals. That was my inheritance. Twelve dusty pieces of pottery sitting on a folding table in the garage. Wanda picked up one of the jars and examined it.
“Honestly, I don’t know why Mama kept these ugly things.” “They were in her kitchen,” I said quietly. “Exactly. Her kitchen. Not an antique shop.”
“At least you got something. Those things might be worth five dollars at a yard sale.”

Wanda placed the jar back on the table. “Fitting, really. The one who never amounted to much gets the junk.” I looked at both of them. I wanted to remind Wanda who had spent the last three years driving forty minutes each way to take Mama to medical appointments.
I wanted to remind Charles who had slept in the hospital chair when Mama broke her hip.
I wanted to remind them who had cleaned her kitchen, washed her sheets, paid her overdue electric bill, and sat beside her when she couldn’t remember what day it was.
But I didn’t. I had learned something during those years.
Some people only remember family when there’s something to inherit. I signed the papers acknowledging receipt of the twelve jars. Then I loaded them into my old sedan. Wanda waved as I drove away.
“Don’t forget to send us pictures when you sell your treasures!” I didn’t look back. That evening, I carried the jars into my little house and placed them on the kitchen counter.
My husband, David, had died six years earlier, and Mama had been the last person in my family who made me feel like I belonged somewhere.
And somehow, my siblings had managed to turn her funeral into a competition over money.
If nothing else, I thought, I could clean the jars and perhaps sell them at a flea market.
Most were ordinary ceramic decorations, the kind people bought at country fairs decades ago.
But when I picked up the largest pig, something felt wrong.
Something solid slid against the inside.
There was a rusted metal lid beneath its belly, almost completely hidden by years of dirt.
I wrapped a towel around the lid and tried again.
With a sharp metallic squeak, the lid loosened.
A small bundle wrapped in an old, moldy dishrag slid into my hand.
Because beneath that dishrag was a small black metal box.
And taped to the top was a yellow envelope.
“For my youngest daughter, Eleanor. Open this only when your brother and sister have taken everything they believe belongs to them.”
For several minutes, I simply stared at the envelope.
It began with five words that made my heart ache.
If you are reading this, then your brother and sister have done exactly what I feared they would do.
They have divided my belongings according to what they believe has value.
Wanda has taken the money and the furniture.
And you have been left with the twelve jars.
They were the only things I could leave you without either of them becoming suspicious.
Do not sign anything else they bring you.
And whatever happens, do not tell them you found this letter.
You have spent your life taking care of everyone else.
Now it is time to take care of yourself.
My fingers trembled as I opened the black box.
A thick envelope containing property documents.
And a photograph of Mama standing beside a younger man I had never seen before.
On the back of the photograph, she had written:
“Your father knew the truth. The land was never Charles’s to inherit.”
My father had died when I was seventeen.
Charles had always told everyone that Dad left the forty acres to the family and that Mama had simply allowed him to manage it.
The third was a document with an official county recording stamp.
The exact forty acres Charles had just inherited.
But the owner listed on the document wasn’t my mother.
It was a company called Bellwood Agricultural Holdings.
And at the bottom was a name that made me stop breathing.
The forty acres, the farmhouse, the barn, and several surrounding parcels had been placed in a trust nearly thirty years earlier.
According to the paperwork, a large portion of the land had been leased to a regional energy company for the construction of a utility and distribution facility.
The annual lease payments had been accumulating in a protected account.
The agreement had been signed twenty-three years earlier.
Even without knowing the exact payment history, the amount could be substantial.
And that wasn’t counting the land itself.
A second envelope was tucked beneath the bank statement.
It contained a letter from an attorney named Harold Bennett.
